source.title_on_document: Evaluating AI-assisted creative ideation: A crossover study in higher education

supplement.where: The document refers to no supplementary material or online appendix. Data availability: 'Data will be made available on request.' (p. 15).

paper_design_summary: In one two-hour session, 51 third-year industrial design engineering students at UPC (Spain) were randomly split into two groups for a crossover: Group A (n = 24) did Task 1 (ideas to improve public transport) unaided and Task 2 (ideas to improve university spaces) with ChatGPT (GPT-3.5); Group B (n = 27) did the reverse. Each task asked for eight handwritten ideas in 30 minutes (728 ideas in total). Researchers scored fluency, flexibility (second-level categories), originality (unique ideas and solutions), novelty (count of ideas resembling existing products), text and image elaboration, thematic diversity indices, and LaBSE semantic divergence.

studies.label: Randomised crossover ideation experiment (public transport and university spaces tasks)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Order of conditions: AI-assisted (ChatGPT GPT-3.5) first then unaided (Group B, n = 27), or unaided first then AI-assisted (Group A, n = 24). Task order was fixed (T1 public transport, T2 university spaces), so condition and task are crossed by group.
assignment.quote: a randomised controlled crossover experiment was employed, in which participants were randomly assigned to one condition for the first task and then switched to the other condition for the second task.
assignment.locator: p. 4, Section 3.2.1; p. 5, Fig. 1; p. 7, Table 3 note (Group A n = 24; Group B n = 27)

arms.name: AI-assisted
arms.description: Computer lab with university computers and internet access limited to ChatGPT (GPT-3.5). Group B in T1 (27 students, 195 ideas); Group A in T2 (24 students, 173 ideas). Every participant did one task in this condition.

arms.name: Unaided
arms.description: Classroom with no computer access and no external resources or electronic devices. Group A in T1 (24 students, 158 ideas); Group B in T2 (27 students, 202 ideas). Every participant did one task in this condition.

participants.exclusions: No exclusions reported. Table 4 note: Unaided n = 51, AI-assisted n = 51; Table 5 note: Group A n = 24, Group B n = 27. For the qualitative analysis only, 49 of 51 ChatGPT conversations were retrieved (p. 10).
participants.who: Third-year students in the bachelor's degree in industrial design engineering and product development, Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya - BarcelonaTech (UPC).
participants.quote: The study involved 51 third-year students from the bachelor's degree in industrial design engineering and product development at the Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya
participants.locator: p. 4, Section 3.1; p. 4-5, Section 3.2.1 ('They were then randomly divided into two groups'); p. 5, Fig. 1; p. 8, Table 4 note

ai_tool.how_used: Free use of ChatGPT in a computer lab during the 30-minute task; students wrote and drew their ideas by hand on pre-printed templates. Prompts were mostly generic requests for ideas (48.39 percent of 341 prompts, Table 9).

task.description: Generate eight innovative ideas, each on a separate sheet with a drawing and description: T1 improving public transport; T2 improving university spaces.
task.duration: 30 minutes per task, within a two-hour session

outcomes.name: Fluency (number of ideas generated per participant)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Total number of ideas generated (Table 2). The task asked for eight ideas, so the measure has a ceiling of about 8. Paper warns fluency violates ANOVA assumptions (p. 6).

contrasts.reported: Unaided 7.06 (1.54) vs AI-assisted 7.22 (1.08), n = 51 each; Wilcoxon signed-rank z = 0.77, p = .439, r = .11
Task 1: Group A unaided 6.58 (1.98) vs Group B AI-assisted 7.22 (1.12); Mann-Whitney U = 374, z = 1.03, p = .304, r = .14

contrasts.control_arm: Group B unaided, Task 2, after AI use in Task 1 (n = 27)
contrasts.reported: Task 2: Group A AI-assisted 7.21 (1.06) vs Group B unaided 7.48 (0.85); Mann-Whitney U = 373, z = 1.06, p = .289, r = .15

outcomes.name: Flexibility (number of second-level categories explored per participant)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Count of second-level (LV2) categories explored, from an inductive three-level categorisation of the 728 anonymised ideas by the researchers, blind to condition, consensus-based (pp. 5-7, Table 2).

contrasts.reported: Unaided 5.51 (1.78) vs AI-assisted 5.57 (1.36), n = 51 each; Wilcoxon signed-rank z = 0.21, p = .833, r = .03
Task 1: Group A unaided 4.58 (1.81) vs Group B AI-assisted 5.67 (1.54); Mann-Whitney U = 440, z = 2.21, p = .027, r = .31

contrasts.control_arm: Group B unaided, Task 2, after AI use in Task 1 (n = 27)
contrasts.reported: Task 2: Group A AI-assisted 5.46 (1.14) vs Group B unaided 6.33 (1.30); Mann-Whitney U = 461, z = 2.65, p = .008, r = .37

outcomes.name: Originality (count of Unique Ideas and Unique Solutions per participant)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Count of Unique Ideas (no other idea in the pooled 728 fits the same LV3 subcategory) plus Unique Solutions (clearly different solution within an LV3 subcategory), coded by the researchers (pp. 5-7, Table 2). Rarity is relative to the full dataset of both conditions.

contrasts.reported: Unaided 3.27 (1.74) vs AI-assisted 2.94 (1.35), n = 51 each; Wilcoxon signed-rank z = -1.24, p = .216, r = .17
Task 1: Group A unaided 2.50 (1.47) vs Group B AI-assisted 3.33 (1.07); Mann-Whitney U = 437, z = 2.20, p = .028, r = .31

contrasts.control_arm: Group B unaided, Task 2, after AI use in Task 1 (n = 27)
contrasts.reported: Task 2: Group A AI-assisted 2.50 (1.50) vs Group B unaided 3.96 (1.70); Mann-Whitney U = 474, z = 2.88, p = .004, r = .40

outcomes.name: Novelty (count of Existing Solutions per participant; a higher count means less novelty)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Count of ideas labelled Existing Solutions (ideas resembling existing products), coded by the researchers; 'A lower number reflects greater novelty' (Table 2). Study-specific measure; paper says it needs validation (p. 13). Sign reversed: direction below is stated for novelty, not for the raw count.

contrasts.reported: Existing Solutions count: Unaided 0.55 (0.81) vs AI-assisted 1.00 (0.96), n = 51 each; Wilcoxon signed-rank z = 2.55, p = .011, r = .36 (more existing solutions, i.e. lower novelty, with AI)

Mixed between-within ANOVA, main effect of AI usage: Wilks' lambda = 0.872, F(1, 49) = 7.19, p = .010, partial eta squared = 0.13; main effect of condition order F(1, 49) = 1.56, p = .218, partial eta squared = 0.03
Existing Solutions, Task 1: Group A unaided 0.67 (0.87) vs Group B AI-assisted 1.07 (1.07); Mann-Whitney U = 392, z = 1.36, p = .172, r = .19

contrasts.control_arm: Group B unaided, Task 2, after AI use in Task 1 (n = 27)
contrasts.reported: Existing Solutions, Task 2: Group A AI-assisted 0.92 (0.83) vs Group B unaided 0.44 (0.75); Mann-Whitney U = 211, z = -2.35, p = .019, r = .33

outcomes.name: Text elaboration (word count of idea descriptions)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Word count of the idea description (Table 2), text extracted by OCR through Gemini with manual verification (p. 7). No scoring model: the code list has no word-count option.

contrasts.reported: Unaided 25.57 (8.06) vs AI-assisted 23.36 (7.66), n = 51 each; Wilcoxon signed-rank z = -2.44, p = .015, r = .34
Task 1: Group A unaided 25.54 (8.92) vs Group B AI-assisted 25.19 (7.14); Mann-Whitney U = 323, z = 0.03, p = .977, r = .00

contrasts.control_arm: Group B unaided, Task 2, after AI use in Task 1 (n = 27)
contrasts.reported: Task 2: Group A AI-assisted 21.31 (7.85) vs Group B unaided 25.60 (7.39); Mann-Whitney U = 444, z = 2.26, p = .024, r = .32

outcomes.name: Image elaboration (three yes/no features of the drawing)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Sum of three binary codes for the drawing: representation of human interaction, of motion or states, and of 3D volume (Table 2). The paper does not say who coded them.

contrasts.reported: Unaided 1.32 (0.36) vs AI-assisted 1.28 (0.40), n = 51 each; Wilcoxon signed-rank z = -0.18, p = .857, r = .03
Task 1: Group A unaided 1.35 (0.35) vs Group B AI-assisted 1.20 (0.43); Mann-Whitney U = 260, z = 1.22, p = .223, r = .17

contrasts.control_arm: Group B unaided, Task 2, after AI use in Task 1 (n = 27)
contrasts.reported: Task 2: Group A AI-assisted 1.36 (0.36) vs Group B unaided 1.29 (0.36); Mann-Whitney U = 279, z = 0.86, p = .389, r = .12

outcomes.name: Group-level semantic divergence (cosine distance of each idea to its condition's centroid, LaBSE)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Idea descriptions OCR'd with Gemini and manually verified, embedded with LaBSE; cosine distance of each idea to the mean embedding of its condition (AI-assisted vs unaided), compared with an independent samples t-test (p. 7, Section 3.3.2). Higher divergence means less homogeneous.

contrasts.reported: Divergence to centroid: unaided M = 0.28 (SD = 0.06), AI-assisted M = 0.29 (SD = 0.07); t(728) = -3.54, p < .001, d = -0.26, 95 % CI [-0.03, -0.01]. The paper interprets this as AI-assisted ideas being 'modestly more semantically similar to the group centroid'.

diversity_detail.metric: Cosine distance to the condition centroid (semantic divergence)
diversity_detail.computed_over: Each idea against the average embedding of all ideas in its condition (AI-assisted vs unaided), pooling both tasks
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Independent samples t-test over ideas (reported df 728)
diversity_detail.notes: Direction conflict: the printed means (AI 0.29 > unaided 0.28), the CI sign, and Fig. 3(a) show higher divergence (more spread) for AI-assisted ideas, but the text and abstract state that semantic divergence was significantly lower with AI (homogenisation). Direction here follows the printed numbers. Centroids pool two different tasks, so task mix within each condition also affects the distances.

outcomes.name: Individual-level semantic divergence (within each participant's own set of ideas, LaBSE)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Methods: 'the average pairwise semantic divergence within each participant's set of ideas was computed per condition' and compared by paired samples t-test (p. 7). Results describe it as 'average semantic divergence from the centroid per participant' (p. 10). Coded as flexibility because it measures variety among one person's own ideas; the paper frames it as individual-level homogenisation.

contrasts.reported: Unaided M = 0.28 (SD = 0.03), AI-assisted M = 0.29 (SD = 0.03); paired t(364) = 3.41, p = .001, d = 0.48, 95 % CI [0.01, 0.03]. The paper interprets this as participants generating 'more semantically concentrated ideas when using AI'.

outcomes.name: Thematic diversity of the condition's idea pool (Shannon and Simpson indices over LV2 and LV3 categories)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Shannon (H') and Simpson (1-D) indices over researcher-coded LV2 and LV3 categories, computed on each condition's pooled ideas; also counts of categories exclusive to each condition (Table 6: LV2 unaided-only 4, mixed 46, AI-only 5; LV3 unaided-only 26, mixed 88, AI-only 29).

contrasts.reported: LV2: unaided 50 categories, H' = 3.538, 1-D = 0.964; AI-assisted 51, H' = 3.661, 1-D = 0.972; difference -0.123 and -0.008. LV3: unaided 114, H' = 4.503, 1-D = 0.990; AI-assisted 117, H' = 4.588, 1-D = 0.992; difference -0.085 and -0.002. No test reported; the paper calls the diversity 'comparable'.

diversity_detail.metric: Shannon index H' and Simpson index 1-D over category frequencies
diversity_detail.computed_over: Each condition's whole pool of ideas (both tasks pooled), at LV2 and LV3 category levels
diversity_detail.notes: Differences are tiny and slightly favour the AI-assisted pool; descriptive only.

outcomes.name: Category size of each idea (clustering in dominant categories)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Size of the category each idea falls in, compared between AI-assisted and unaided ideas by Mann-Whitney U (pp. 7, 10). A larger size means more clustering in shared themes.

contrasts.reported: Category size: AI-assisted N = 368, M = 4.22, SD = 3.01; unaided N = 360, M = 4.58, SD = 3.65; U = 65,489, z = -0.27, p = .798

diversity_detail.metric: Mean size of the category containing each idea
diversity_detail.computed_over: Each idea's category size in the pooled categorisation of all 728 ideas
diversity_detail.notes: The paper does not say at which level (LV2 or LV3) category size is computed.

outcomes.name: Unique contributions (Unique Ideas and Unique Solutions) by condition
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Whether each idea is a Unique Idea or Unique Solution relative to all 728 ideas, compared by chi-square tests; the paper treats a lower frequency of unique contributions as thematic homogenisation (p. 4). Same coding as the originality score in S1-O3, at idea level.

contrasts.reported: Table 6: unaided UI 85, US 82, ES 28; AI-assisted UI 81, US 69, ES 51. Total unique contributions chi2(1, N = 728) = 2.12, p = .145; Unique Ideas chi2(1, N = 728) = 0.18, p = .670; Unique Solutions chi2(1, N = 728) = 1.56, p = .212

diversity_detail.metric: Counts of Unique Ideas and Unique Solutions per condition
diversity_detail.computed_over: Each idea classified against all 728 ideas from both conditions

outcomes.name: Flexibility on the unaided task after prior AI use (order effect)
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Same LV2 count as S1-O2, on the unaided task of Group B (T2, after using AI in T1). The paper tests the order effect as the condition x order interaction in a mixed between-within ANOVA. No direct test of Group B T2 unaided against Group A T1 unaided is reported, and the two use different tasks.
outcomes.delay: Second 30-minute task in the same two-hour session

contrasts.treatment_arm: Group B unaided in Task 2, after AI in Task 1 (n = 27)
contrasts.control_arm: Group A unaided in Task 1, no prior AI (n = 24)
contrasts.reported: Unaided means: Group B T2 6.33 (1.30) vs Group A T1 4.58 (1.81) (Table 5; different tasks, no direct test). Mixed ANOVA condition x order interaction: Wilks' lambda = 0.801, F(1, 49) = 12.19, p = .001, partial eta squared = 0.20

outcomes.name: Originality on the unaided task after prior AI use (order effect)
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Same Unique Ideas plus Unique Solutions count as S1-O3, on Group B's unaided T2 task after AI in T1. Order effect tested as the condition x order interaction. The paper reports no significant interaction for fluency, novelty, text or image elaboration (p. 8).
outcomes.delay: Second 30-minute task in the same two-hour session

contrasts.treatment_arm: Group B unaided in Task 2, after AI in Task 1 (n = 27)
contrasts.control_arm: Group A unaided in Task 1, no prior AI (n = 24)
contrasts.reported: Unaided means: Group B T2 3.96 (1.70) vs Group A T1 2.50 (1.47) (Table 5; different tasks, no direct test). Mixed ANOVA condition x order interaction: Wilks' lambda = 0.747, F(1, 49) = 16.62, p < .001, partial eta squared = 0.25

company_involvement.description: No specific funding; authors declare no competing interests. ChatGPT is the tool studied, with no OpenAI involvement stated.
company_involvement.locator: p. 15, Funding and Declaration of competing interest

data_and_code.data_url: Not posted: 'Data will be made available on request.' (p. 15)

eligibility.reason: Within-person crossover in which students were randomly assigned to the order of ChatGPT-assisted and unaided ideation (p. 4); 51 students analyzed (Table 4 note, n = 51 per condition), just above the 50-person threshold; outcomes (fluency, flexibility, originality, novelty, elaboration, semantic divergence) are scored on the ideas produced. The first-period comparison (Task 1, 27 AI vs 24 unaided) is also a clean between-person randomized contrast.

one_line_finding: With ChatGPT, 51 design engineering students produced more ideas resembling existing products (Existing Solutions 1.00 vs 0.55, Wilcoxon p = .011) and shorter descriptions (23.36 vs 25.57 words, p = .015), with no difference in fluency, flexibility, or originality (Table 4, p. 8); the AI-first group scored higher in flexibility and originality in both tasks (Table 5, p. 9).
open_questions: Semantic divergence direction: the printed means (AI 0.29 vs unaided 0.28 at both levels), CI signs, and Fig. 3 show higher divergence for AI-assisted ideas, yet the abstract and text say divergence was significantly lower with AI. Which is correct?
Degrees of freedom: group-level t(728) with 728 ideas (expected 726) and individual-level paired t(364) with 51 participants. The individual-level test may treat ideas, not participants, as the unit.
Individual-level divergence is described as average pairwise divergence in Methods (p. 7) and as divergence from the centroid in Results (p. 10).

Task is fixed by period (T1 public transport, T2 university spaces), so the pooled within-person AI contrast relies on counterbalancing of order; order effects for flexibility and originality are large, so the pooled Table 4 contrast mixes AI and order/task effects.
Whether 51 is the count at assignment: the paper says 51 students were involved and were randomly divided into two groups; no exclusions are mentioned.
notes: Single study, single session, single institution. Fluency has a ceiling because the task asked for eight ideas. All idea categorisation (flexibility, originality, novelty, thematic diversity) was done by the researchers on anonymised ideas, blind to condition, with consensus rather than measured agreement (p. 5). No human creativity ratings. Qualitative analysis of 341 prompts from 49 retrieved conversations (Tables 8-9) is not coded as an outcome. The Task 2 between-group contrast (Group A AI vs Group B unaided after AI) is recorded with comparison_type 'other' because the control group had used AI in Task 1.
